content: Manual fetal manipulation has been proposed as a method to enhance the efficiency of fetal heart rate testing during pregnancy. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits or harms associated with using manual fetal manipulation alongside tests of fetal wellbeing. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of September 30, 2013. The review included all randomized controlled trials, both published and unpublished, that compared manual fetal manipulation to mock stimulation, no stimulation, or other forms of stimulation in conjunction with cardiotocography or other fetal wellbeing tests. Three independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the quality of the trials, and extracted relevant data. The accuracy of the data was verified, and additional information was sought from the authors of the included trials. The review included four trials involving a total of 1,280 women and 2,670 testing episodes. None of the trials were free from bias across all domains, and only two trials demonstrated low risk of bias in both selection and attrition categories. Manual fetal manipulation was associated with a reduction in the occurrence of non-reactive antenatal cardiotocography tests when compared to mock or no stimulation. However, this reduction was not statistically significant (average risk ratio [RR] 0.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 6.20, I² = 96%; two trials, N = 2,350). Additionally, there was no significant decrease in the average time required to achieve a reactive cardiotocography result (mean difference -2.29 minutes, 95% CI -9.61 to 5.03 minutes, I² = 97%; two trials, N = 560). When comparing manual fetal manipulation to vibroacoustic stimulation, no significant differences were observed in the rates of non-reactive cardiotocography or the need for contraction-stress testing. Furthermore, no data were available regarding other important outcomes, such as perinatal mortality, fetal distress, maternal anxiety, or gestational age at delivery. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to support the routine use of manual fetal manipulation during cardiotocography or other tests of fetal wellbeing. Further research using standardized protocols is necessary to better understand the potential role of manual fetal manipulation in this context.
